utterances.text: Well, whether there was audio accompanying the video-clip during my proofing, perhaps the Prosecutor can help us. I can't really recall. I do recall that there were some problems, but I can't even recall if shown the transcript. Maybe the Prosecutor can be of assistance here, because he proofed me and he showed me the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the Prosecutor is free to assist you, if he so chooses, later on. But can you just explain to the Trial Chamber whether this would be something that you could see in reality or whether this video-clip was doctored? Now, do you remember -- and whether you remember whether there was an audio with the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall that there was any audio or whether there was a transcript that I saw, which I just saw this briefly. We did not dwell on it, and I can't really recollect anything. It was very brief, so I can't remember; not even from the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While you're trying to refresh your memory, I would like to show you 1D265. Could we please pull up 1D265.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Exhibit D92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We've already seen this document, and I quoted some portions that I wanted to refer you to. Now, please take a look. This is a criminal report, and there's a list of persons there who were identified. Let's just read the first name. We don't have to read the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Mehmedalija Cavcic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And so on and so forth. There is information and personal details for all the people on the list. Now, please, can we see the end of this list, or, rather, can we just scroll it so that the witness can read through it and whether he can then confirm for us whether all these individuals were local people from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say -- when we say "Zepa," we imply two municipalities, Han Pijesak and Rogatica. In the beginning, they were separate, but only after the take-over of all of the villages, for all practical purposes, in Han Pijesak municipality, and those people then moved to Zepa, only then did it become one thing, Zepa. And those are individuals from the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Now, can we move on to the next page, please, when the witness indicates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. Can we move on? Next page. Next page, please. Next page, please, if there are any more pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think this will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So who are these individuals? These individuals were included in the criminal report against those individuals in the Zepa enclave who were identified as perpetrators when 43 soldiers were killed and others taken prisoner. Could we now please see 1D267.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please give this hard copy to the witness, because it is a handwritten document, so that he can take a look at 1D267. And we will have it on our screens, but it's hard to read from it. And then perhaps the witness can tell us whether all these individuals were members of the Zepa Brigade or the brigade of the Zepa enclave. And I will tell you where this list comes from. This list was received from the Yugoslav Army, and it shows members of the Zepa Brigade who crossed over to the Yugoslav territory and then moved on to third countries, in agreement with the International Red Cross, which provided guarantees for their movement -- freedom of movement and settlement. Now, could we please see pages 234 and 5 for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, because the witness has the hard copy and he can easily leaf through it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, the hard copy was shown to the Chamber first, and now the witness has the opportunity to look at it. And later on, it should be forwarded to the Prosecution as well. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a copy of -- a hard copy already. Thank you. But I do want to raise an issue with respect to this document and with respect to 1D00274, which we saw earlier, the letter from Alija Izetbegovic to the UN in New York. It's the same query I had with respect to the document we saw yesterday that bore no ERN and we have no information about the source of this document, its pedigree, so to speak, or where it emanates from. All we've heard is that it's a list, allegedly, of brigade members. We don't have a translation. I note that it -- my rudimentary understanding of the language suggests that some of these people listed here as civilians. So if we could have some proffer as to, again, where this document comes from, how it was provided, because it bears no ERN, no -- it certainly didn't come from us, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would suggest that you prepare some additional information we would like to hear after the second break. It is now the time for the second break, and you should consider this request by Mr. Thayer during the break. We adjourn, and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask this: Perhaps the witness can keep this hard copy so that he can leaf through it during the break. Would that be all right? That's all I have to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is no problem. It will save time. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Our apologies for the delay. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have a question for the witness. I provided him with a list of the soldiers from Zepa who moved to Serbia under the auspices of the ICRC. Before that, we saw the criminal report containing 149 names, so that he would be able to see whether the people were from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on the criminal report list of 149, can you tell us whether you saw anyone there who was not from Zepa? And on the paper copy I gave you containing that list there, were there any people there who were not from Zepa and who crossed over into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is two questions, I believe. The first list I saw on the screen contains the names of people from Zepa. The other list I received in hard copy also includes the names of people from the enclave of Zepa, although I saw that a few of them were born in Srebrenica. I must say, though, that two villages surrounding Srebrenica belonged to the municipality of Zepa. They received humanitarian assistance from us. So I would say that these people were from the enclave of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the first list of 149, we saw that Benjamin Kulovac was also included, and the report was submitted against him as well. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember why the Prosecutor asked you why Benjamin Kulovac was afraid to appear at another meeting, and could that be the reason why he ended up on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he knew at all at the time. Well, this criminal report was submitted by Serb authorities, and what we had in our hands there was a military conflict. It's a legal matter, and I don't know whether that can fall under the -- under a criminal report. In any case, Benjamin Kulovac was not aware of any criminal reports being submitted against him at that time. He was afraid, though, but I don't know why. Perhaps you should ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Irrespective of everything that happened, did he join those wounded on their way to Sarajevo? Was he let to pass through by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He joined the first convoy with the wounded. He was let through by the Serb side and reached Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us go back to that part where you spoke about your arrest. We can see that all these people were from the enclave of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Could one of the reasons for the fear be the issue of the 43 Serbs who were killed? Was that, perhaps, one of the reasons for the fear of the soldiers, due to which they wouldn't surrender or cross RS territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is possible. It could have been one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the witness's statement, which is 1D248. Please, do not broadcast the cover page or the witness's name. We can immediately go to page 8, paragraph 5, the last three lines. Thank you. Please do not broadcast this page publicly. Let us go to page 8, paragraph 5, the last three lines. Thank you. We can see it in the Serbian. It is the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will start with the second line from the bottom: "In the meantime, the Serb soldiers enter the center of Zepa. Amir Imamovic, who was brought in together with Hajric, was another Presidency member. They asked us to exercise much greater pressure so that the able-bodied men would surrender. Hajric was ordered to go to the mountains, where the headquarters of our army was, to ask them to surrender." It is page 9, the first two lines of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have that. It further reads: "They asked us to exercise much greater pressure so that the able-bodied men would surrender. Hajric was told to go to the mountains, where our headquarters were, to ask them to surrender."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This was in your statement. Do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since this concerns members of the War Presidency, and since we discussed the agreement and its signing, the agreement on the disarmament of the soldiers, which was a precondition for the implementation of all the other provisions, was it not only logical that the War Presidency members who signed the agreement, to sign also the decision invoked here by the OTP of the 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember that decision, and I said that it was signed under pressure. I repeat that even such a signed decision had no effective power over any military decisions. This is what I continually stress. All these members of the Presidency, all three of us, who signed under pressure, I assert, could not exercise any control. It had no value. It wasn't able to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it not normal for three men to decide on something that would follow the items of the agreement, rather than sending the whole of the VRS up Mount Zepa to kill off all the soldiers there? What would have been better, that two members of the War Presidency go and visit the Army of B and H soldiers or to continue fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the way you put your question begs me to say yes. But none of these War Presidency members, and I don't know whether you knew that, could have done anything about it. We could sign anything you wanted, but we couldn't implement it, and that's the essence of it. The way you put your question, whether it would have been better, yes, it would have, but it was not viable. All three of us who were there had no effective control over that issue. And in my view, no one else in Zepa did on the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you agree with me that the party included in negotiations, drafting an agreement, cannot know what the scope of your authority is over any soldiers? Are you honest when you say that? We couldn't have known whether you had any influence or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, legally and formally speaking, that is so, but let me go back to the agreement I signed. I said orally that as regards the army, I do not have the legitimacy or authority necessary. I could guarantee only the implementation pertaining to civilians. You, as the Serb side, could have said, Well, thank you very much, we're not interested in that. In that case, there probably would have not been any evacuation of civilians. But it was logical of you to expect that on the other end of the table you would have someone who could cover all of the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it not a more peaceful option to have the War Presidency draft a decision of the 27th and show it to the soldiers in Zepa for their acceptance? If they don't want to, they can go on fighting. Was it not a peaceful option, or should have been for the armed option from the outset?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's always best to avoid any conflict, but I know how people reasoned. There was this fear, and that was what prevented the implementation of that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But was it necessary to disarm the civil population, in particular the able-bodied men, in the demilitarised zone, in keeping with the agreement, and that's why the decision was made? We all know what the fate of the soldiers was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was necessary to lay down arms, to have it a weapon-free zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order to implement the agreement on the disarmament of the soldiers, we needed a previous decision to have been made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't following.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you recall the title of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Agreement on the Disarmament of Soldiers," I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No, "Able-Bodied Men." Was it not logical that the War Presidency should issue a decision on disarmament in order to implement the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You, when you were arrested, were you arrested for not implementing the agreement and for failing to implement your party's obligations, including disarmament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was expressly stated, but it was my assessment that I was arrested because we did not secure the disarmament of able-bodied men in Zepa, and I was one of the signatories.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to page 9, paragraph 2. We will read out the first four lines for your benefit, because we need to refresh your memory: "On the 27th of July, Imamovic and I, who were held in the same room. An hour and a half after the last convoy was allowed to proceed, Serb military police entered the UNPROFOR house with a Serb officer, and they informed us that we were arrested for noncompliance of paragraph 8 of the agreement."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This statement was made rather early on, so I can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you were told that you were arrested for noncompliance with the agreement; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if I go by my statement, it appears to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were any civilians held there who were on the last bus because of this noncompliance with the agreement about the evacuation of civilians and able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know they were taken off the bus and held there, but I don't know what the reason was. I hear it from you, what the reason may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you last time, and perhaps we needn't go back to the document because you also said that in your statement -- you said that General Mladic let all the buses pass, except the last one, when the passengers were held there, and you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you registered the next day, on the 28th, by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on the 28th. I think it was either the 30th of July or the 1st of August, and it was in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The next paragraph, line 4, you say: "The next day, we were registered by the Red Cross." And just above that, in the previous paragraph, you mention the 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but before that I say I don't know whether on the 30th or the 31st of July we were transferred to Rogatica. Upon my arrival there, the next day we were registered. So it wasn't on the 28th. You should read the paragraph preceding that one, its last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "In Rogatica, they took us to a facility used as a prison. There was some 40 people there who were taken off the bus in the last convoy." And then you say that you were registered by the Red Cross. Did they register these 40 people as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order to be fair, in a part of your statement you said that Rajko Pusic was the prison commander. I don't think you meant that. Perhaps this was a mistake, because the brigade commander could not have been acting as prison warden. It was probably one of his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how this made its way into the statement, but he was not the prison warden. It was another gentleman, a Neskovic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. In any case, they may have been his subordinates from the brigade. Were they all from Rogatica or from some other level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was the Rogatica Military Police that secured the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will not now go to the supplemental statement, because it says "Draft Version" across it. But just tell us, please, why was it necessary for you to provide this supplemental draft version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can barely remember that. Do you mean the supplement to this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. It is appended to this statement. It contains nine paragraphs, and it also includes photographs where you identified certain individuals. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that was in the additional interview conducted by the investigator, and I don't know how all of that transpired. But it was about 10 years ago. That was when they brought all those photos for me to identify the individuals depicted on them. That's where that other statement comes from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could -- I would like to move and tender 1D273 and 65 ter 06417 into evidence, although I did not want to show them here today, both in order to save some time and also because of the measures that were here in place for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm a little bit confused. I saw that you used three documents, 1D248, and this is the OTP statement of the witness, 1D274 and not 3, 1D267. Now you are referring to other numbers. I have no idea what these are. Could you explain this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D273 and 65 ter 06417, these are video-clips that I'm proposing to move into evidence. And then, after that, we will discuss these other documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me take the second exhibit first, 65 ter 06417. That is a proposed Prosecution exhibit which is a compilation video based on several other separate videos which contain extended footage of these meetings, some of which the Trial Chamber has already seen. Parts of those videos have yet to be played. What we did was instead of having each individual video in its entirety played before the Trial Chamber, we combined portions of those videos into what we have called the Zepa compilation video, and that's why we gave it a separate 65 ter number. We showed some -- as the Court remembers, some portions of 6417, but we haven't shown the entire thing. That's why we did not tender 6417, since it includes portions which have yet to be played before the Trial Chamber. So I'm not sure which portion of 6417 General Tolimir is intending to tender at this point because I, frankly, can't remember -- I think some portions may have been played, but I just don't know right now. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we then see this video compilation that was shown here to all of us so that we can use it with other witnesses as well, because it was publicly shown and it's also in the transcript? So that's what we are asking and seeking to tender, whatever was shown here, and what is in the video, and what was recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's now a little bit difficult just to play the video again, to identify numbers and -- 65 ter numbers, and to decide about the admission of this video. I'm not sure, Mr. Thayer. Perhaps you can help us. Did you tender this compilation of videos?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, we did not, Mr. President, for the reasons I've explained. Perhaps what we can do is maintain it MFI'd, and when the Defence is able to identify the time codes, then we can note that for the record, rather than introducing it twice or introducing a separate clip of it, which just unnecessarily creates exhibits, when we've got the whole thing in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is a good proposal, Mr. Thayer. 65 ter 6417 will be marked for identification, and I would invite both parties to discuss which parts of it should be, at the end of the day, really admitted into evidence. Both parties should use it with other witnesses as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'm confident that the entire compilation video will be played to witnesses and ultimately will be tendered, so I think it's, at the end of the day, a moot issue. Now, with respect to the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. We would like to have it MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First we have to decide will it be -- will it have a P number or a D number? It was produced by the Prosecution, who we think will tender it one day. If you don't object to that, it should get a P number. And it is necessary to give the DVD to the Registry so that we have a clear record of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Not to be too possessive, but it is our compilation. We worked hard on it, so that would be fine. The Defence has been supplied with a copy of that DVD, with an explanation of the underlying videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, Mr. Tolimir, with this procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, we absolutely agree with your ruling, and I think it is in both our interests. I have a few more questions for the witness, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I do have this request. 1D273 is our video that was shown here. If you recall, we provided the transcript for it, and we would appreciate this video being marked for identification or admitted into evidence. And I will just remind you that this was from the negotiations, the words pronounced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 65 ter 6417 will be marked for identification with a P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 6417 will be Exhibit P740, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, to avoid any misunderstandings and confusion during the trial, I was told that 1D273 is part of the document we just have marked as P740. Mr. Gajic, you don't agree. Please explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the compilation video does not contain the excerpt from the meeting of 19th of July, 1995. We showed the portion to the witness that is not included in the compilation video tendered by the Prosecution, and that is why we are seeking to tender it as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be marked for identification as well with a D number. Yes, we would like to receive the D number, and then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D273 will be Exhibit D18, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Two issues with respect to that exhibit, Mr. President. The first is: That footage that was shown actually is already in evidence as P593 that also has a transcript for it. We saw the Defence put together their own B/C/S transcript. I don't think it was translated into English. But P593, which came in through, I believe, Colonel Fortin, does have a transcript. My second query is: With respect to 1D273, we don't have an objection to it. It is superfluous, but we don't know where -- what the source of that footage is. It looks the same, but I notice that there were some inter-spliced images that don't appear anywhere else in the footage that we've seen over the years. The Trial Chamber may recall we see the scene of the meeting at the table, and all of a sudden there are a bunch of soldiers sitting on a tank or something, and that raises, in my mind, the question of, again, what's the provenance of the video. No objection, but we want to know where it came from, because that's footage that comes in with no explanation or context. It may be a compilation of their own or taken from a news source, and so that may explain it, but we've got no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the surrogate sheet with that video, Mr. President, it is clearly indicated what the provenance of this video is. There is an ERN number. In other words, it is a Prosecution video. And this video, too, was used by the Prosecution for their compilation video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see there is disagreement, but it is not necessary to discuss it further at this point in time. I would like to ask the Defence: Are you tendering 1D248? This is the OTP statement of the witness. You used it yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First, a correction for the record. 65 ter 1D273 is Exhibit D108, marked for identification. 65 ter 1D248 will be Exhibit D109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you're all a little confused now. I would like to deal with 1D274 and 1D267. I think these were the documents Mr. Thayer asked for further clarification about the source, and where it comes from, and so on. I would like to know if you are tendering these two documents. If you will do that, we will only mark them for identification, and we would like, like we did with another document yesterday, to ask for a written submission with a clear definition where these documents come from and what is the background of it. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as for 65 ter documents 1D274 and 1D269, these, in fact, are in the book of Sefer Halilovic's entitled "State Secret." This book was published in 2005, and it contains a wealth of documents. I contacted the Prosecutor yesterday and was provided a batch of documents from the BH Army, and it was explained to me that those documents were attached to this book. And that is why across this document there is this marking which says "State Secret." And as for Samir Halilovic, he was the son of General Halilovic, Sefer Halilovic, who was the commander of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm not sure which prosecutor we're talking about. It's not an OTP Prosecutor. Maybe a prosecutor from Serbia. But we have no knowledge about this, just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I would like to clarify. Are you talking about 1D267 or 1D269?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have to say that there was an error in the transcript, or in the translation, actually. I never mentioned the Prosecution. I mentioned the source; in other words, the person who provided these documents to me. We are referring to 1D274. This is a letter from Alija Izetbegovic to the UN Security Council. And the second document is D102, marked for identification, which relates to the general mobilisation call-up in Zepa. And these documents were, in fact, attachments in the book of Samir Halilovic entitled "State Secret."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. I'm not sure if this is sufficient, but we can't continue in this way. Yesterday, I asked you for a written submission and explanation so that we can receive comment by the OTP as well. The second one was marked for identification. Now you are asking for 1D -- again the number, please. 1D74 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D274.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, and we would like to receive a written explanation about the source. And if I'm not mistaken, you used 1D267 just before the last break. Are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we're tendering that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I will just ask the witness, and I'm referring to the hard copy that he has: Is any of those individuals that you say are from Zepa -- was any of those persons killed in the Zepa fighting or in the mountains around Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean the people from this list? Well, there were some members of the BH Army who were killed during the military attacks on Zepa. As far as I know, of all these people who crossed over to Serbia from the list, only one young man - I think he tried to escape - he was shot. And as for the rest, they all moved on to third countries, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were there any able-bodied men killed by the VRS after they surrendered, with the exclusion of Avdo Palic, Amir Imamovic, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the third name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- who were killed, and you can tell us when and how and whether they, too, were killed in some war operations or after the war operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you asked me several questions, so I'll try to go one by one. I don't know who was killed in military operations. Now, after August 25th, from what I learned later on, most of these people from this list here moved to Serbia or crossed over to Serbia, except for one man. I heard that he panicked, tried to run, and he was shot. As for the rest, some of them tried to cross over and then were either killed, because they had to go through -- they had to cross the front-line. I don't know how many people were killed. Most of them did cross over near Kladanj. As for those who were taken prisoner, they were taken away and later killed. They were Mehmed Hajric, Amir Imamovic, and later on I heard also that the same was the case with Colonel Avdo Palic. And to the best of my knowledge, there was another man. I don't know if he was a member of the army, but he was an elderly man who was held in Rogatica, in detention, and was taken away by someone. To this day, his remains have not been recovered. And from what I could read in our press, I assume that Lukic from Visegrad took him away and nothing more was known about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What's his name? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, his last name was Cocalic, but I can't say with any certainty. I only heard about this. In any case, it is known that his body was never found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Save for these four people you mentioned as having been killed outside combat later on in August and September, were there any others killed outside combat who actually had come from Zepa and who were men of military age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know everything, because I spent six months in prison. I don't know whether someone was caught and killed trying to cross over. I can neither deny nor confirm that. This is the extent of information I have. As for any others who may have been captured by the VRS and later on killed, that is something I can say nothing about. I cannot say that there were any or that there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While I was in Zepa, while we negotiated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In that period, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When did you hear of Avdo Palic being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was released from prison. It was in January 1996. At that time, he was considered a missing person. I presume a missing person is anyone whose body has never been found. And I heard stories about his capture. It lasted between 1996 and 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge when -- about when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your answer, please, and then no further question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you have information when Avdo Palic and the other two were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Much later, in Bosnia and Sarajevo, it was the main topic when Colonel Palic's disappearance was discussed. According to the final journalistic reports, it appears that Avdo Palic had been killed in early September 1995. They based that conclusion on the examination of his remains. The other two men, there is a witness statement regarding their death. I confirm that they were taken around mid-July, and, according to that witness's statement -- sorry, they were taken in mid-August, and the witness states that in late August they were taken out of the room where they were held captive together with him. It is presumed that they were killed then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just seek to tender D267 into evidence so as to reflect the fact that there were no men of military age who were killed out of those on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are six minutes over time. It's exactly the same amount of time we were delayed when we started, so that you had the full session. Both exhibits will be marked for identification. That means 1D274, I pronounced that already. And 1D267, the list in hard copy shown to the witness, marked for identification, but only admitted at a later stage, after having received additional information about the source, as requested by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D274 will be Exhibit D110, marked for identification. 1D267 will be Exhibit D111, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, have you any indication how much time you need for finishing your cross-examination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if the witness must leave, I'm ready to thank him for his time already now. We discussed most of the topics covered in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, you misunderstand. I just want to know how much time you need. You know the Prosecution used more time than indicated in the examination-in-chief. Therefore, no time pressure on you. I just want to know. And the witness can't leave today because the OTP has some re-examination, I suppose. What is your estimation of the time you still need for cross-examination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will conclude my cross-examination during the first session tomorrow. Therefore, I have five or six questions left. I would like to thank the witness for his co-operation and the answers he provided, as well as all those who assisted us in bringing this testimony to a close. I'd like to thank you and the interpreters as well on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you are in the bad position that you have to return to court tomorrow again. We are sitting in the morning, if I'm not mistaken, in this courtroom. And we thank you for your patience you have with the parties and with the Chamber. We adjourn and resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of September, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.56 p.m.,
